newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parties campaign on growth, tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Polish parties campaign on growth, tax cuts.

text.p: Poland's leading political parties, the ruling ex-communists and the rightist Solidarity alliance, vowed pro-growth policies and tax cuts if they won the September 21 elections but remained divided over religion and abortion.

The ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and the opposition Solidarity Election Action (AWS), which held party conventions on Sunday, both promised measures to curb inflation, cut unemployment, speed privatisation and continue efforts to bring Poland into the European Union and NATO.

But while the SLD, in power since 1993 along with the Peasant Party, said it would adocate a secular state and a right of women to have abortions, the pro-church Solidarity stressed pro-family and traditionalist values.

The SLD, under a slogan of "Good today, better tomorrow," claimed claimed credit for the country's economic success and promised a 25 percent economic growth in the next four years and a radical inflation cut if they win the polls.

It said would strive to boost industrial output by 40 percent, curb inflation to about six percent form 14.6 percent in May and bring the private sector's contribution to gross domestic product to 75-80 percent from the current 60 percent.
"The SLD promises...a continued growth and solving social problems," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told a news conference after the convention.
"I am convinced that just as we have brough Poland to the threshold of the European Union, we will be able to bring it to the full membership," he said.

The AWS, which groups more than 30 small right-wing parties around the Solidarity trade union, said it would restore honesty to public life and combine pro-growth policies with social justice and Christian values.

The group, whose many members helped defeat communism in 1989 but lost power to ex-communists four years later due to internal quarrels, launched slogans "Always: Poland, Freedom, Family" and "The Right Poland."

"The right Poland means fidelity to true values, rightness of people in power, right to private ownership, economic freedom and effective law," AWS leader Marian Krzaklewski said in opening the convention in the central city of Radom.

The AWS says that the economy could be helped not only by the promised measures of tax cuts and quicker privatisation, but also by reducing the role of former communists in many banks and large corporations.
The AWS say that the ex-communists' involvement in the former oppresive regime should make them unfit to govern.

The ex-communists said they would achieve their economic goals by attracting more foreign investors through offering them more investment reliefs, cutting taxes and developing telecoms and road infrastructure.

The Solidarity's programme provides for speedily returning to former owners assets conficated during the cummunist rule and distributing privatisation coupons to all Poles, which would enable them to participate in the country's economic success.

In the process which the Solidarity calls "enfranchisement," the coupons could be exchanged for shares of firms undergoing privatisation and allocated to independent pension funds, to be created under a social security reform plan.
Recent opinion polls have shown the two groups enjoy a similar support of more than 20 percent, suggesting smaller parties could hold a balance of power in the next parliament.
Cimoszewicz said that after the elections, the ex-communists would be ready to consider other government coalition than that with its current partner, the Peasants.
The party has earlier made clear a coalition was also possible with the centrist Union for Freedom and the leftist Labour Union.
The AWS mulls a coalition with a right-radical Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP) and the Union for Freedom.
